title: Keeping ducks alongside chickens
subtitle: Ducks and chickens can share a run, but ducks will make the ground wet and the water messy faster than any other bird you could keep.
excerpt: Mixed poultry flocks of ducks and chickens are common on smallholdings. They work provided you manage the water situation, ducks need to submerge their bill and nostrils to feed safely, and the resulting mess affects chicken bedding and run conditions. Here is how to structure the setup, the feed, and the daily routine to make it work.

glossaryTerms.definition: The feeding behaviour of ducks, who submerge their bill in water and sieve it through lamellae to filter food. Ducks need enough water to submerge their nostrils as well as their bill to clear feed from the nasal passages — preventing sinusitis.

content.text: Ducks and chickens have different water requirements, and this is the relationship's central management challenge. Chickens need water to drink. Ducks need water deep enough to
: they scoop feed mixed with water through their bill and need to clear their nostrils in the process. A nipple drinker that suits chickens perfectly will give a duck chronic sinusitis within a week.

Give ducks a separate, deeper water source sited in the least important corner of the run, somewhere that can get thoroughly muddy without causing problems. A bucket, rubber trough, or purpose-made duck drinker at least 15 cm deep is adequate. Ducks do not need a pond to be healthy, but they need that minimum water depth at the drinker.

Change the duck water at least twice a day in warm weather. Ducks will fill it with wet feed, feathers, and mud within hours. A dirty duck drinker is also used as a swimming pool, making the surrounding ground boggy and creating a welfare issue for the chickens bedding nearby.

Chickens and ducks can share the same pellets, an unmedicated layers' pellet (14-16% protein) works for both. Ducks need more niacin than chickens, and a duck fed on chick crumbs alone will develop leg problems. Standard layers' pellets contain adequate niacin for ducks; specific duck pellets contain more but are not essential if feeding layers' pellets.

Ducks eat by scooping pellets into their bill with water. If you use a hanging feeder designed for chickens, place a trough of water immediately below it so the ducks can wet the pellets. Without water access at the feeder, ducks eat poorly and may impropriate the pellets, pushing them out of the feeder rather than eating them.

Ducks do not roost. They sleep at ground level, so a standard chicken coop with perches serves them poorly. In a mixed flock, provide a separate sleeping area at floor level, a low, three-sided shelter with deep straw works, within or adjacent to the chicken coop.
Ducks lay at night or early morning, usually in a nest scraped in the ground rather than in a nesting box. If collecting duck eggs daily, learn where the duck sleeps, that is where the egg will be.

Chickens and ducks mostly ignore each other in a well-spaced run. Ducks are indifferent to the chicken pecking order and will walk through the middle of a dispute without taking sides. Drakes become a problem in a mixed flock if they attempt to mate with hens, drake mating behaviour is rough and can injure or drown chickens. Keep an eye on any drake that shows interest in hens; separate if it becomes persistent.
